name: Jackson Square
label: Jackson Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jackson Square' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27844554: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jackson Square' (206 m across).
notes: The historic heart of the French Quarter, with the equestrian statue of Andrew Jackson.

text.description:
Jackson Square is the old heart of the French Quarter, a tidy park laid out with iron fences, walkways, benches and Parisian-style planting. It was once the military parade ground known as the Place d'Armes, and it was renamed in 1851 for Andrew Jackson, the hero of the 1815 Battle of New Orleans. A statue of him on horseback stands in the middle, put up in 1856. The square became a National Historic Landmark in 1960 and is also where Louisiana became US territory in 1803.

It photographs well because everything is arranged around one view. On the north side, St. Louis Cathedral sits in the centre, with the Cabildo to its left and the Presbytère to its right. The long red-brick Pontalba Buildings run along the other two sides, which gives you strong lines to frame with.

For a quieter, closer picture, walk north across the grass towards the cathedral. From there you get the cathedral facade low and close, with lawns and paths in the foreground. If you want the whole square in one frame, the Moon Walk on the levee gives a wide view with the cathedral spires centred behind it. Washington Artillery Park, between Decatur Street and the Moon Walk, gives a slightly raised riverside angle. The square is free to enter but can be very busy, and the shop signs along the Pontalba ground floors can clutter a frame, so tilt your phone slightly upwards or step sideways to leave them out.
text.geographic_location: Jackson Square is in the French Quarter of New Orleans, facing St. Louis Cathedral on one side and Decatur Street and the Mississippi levee on the other. Café du Monde is diagonally across Decatur Street from it.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; head for the French Quarter and walk to St. Louis Cathedral. The square is the park directly in front of it. Chartres, St. Peter and St. Ann streets beside the square are closed to traffic, so the final approach is on foot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the cathedral from the grass. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the paths and greenery in the foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spires and the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there the cathedral is ahead of you on the north side, with the park's greenery and paths in front of it. For a closer, lower view of the facade, walk north across the grass towards the cathedral. For a wide alternative with the whole square in view, try the Moon Walk on the levee.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the cathedral on the centre line, keeping the verticals straight. Include a path or a strip of lawn at the bottom of the frame to add depth. Crouching a little makes the foreground look larger. For a wide shot of the whole square, try the Moon Walk instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus and drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. The ultra-wide (0.5x) can stretch and tilt the buildings near the edges, so keep the cathedral near the middle.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning if you can, as the square is often crowded later in the day. Soft, low light is kinder to the facade than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The square is a free, open public park, but the cathedral and museums around it have their own visiting rules, so check the official sites before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter in Jackson Square.
Soft, low morning light suits the cathedral facade better than harsh midday sun.
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch and tilt buildings near the edges of the frame.
The Moon Walk is on the levee and gives a wide view of the square with the cathedral spires behind it.
The cathedral and museums may have their own visiting rules.

name: Bourbon Street
label: Bourbon Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bourbon Street' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Bourbon Street and Iberville Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18544685: large area 'Bourbon Street' (1550 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The famous nightlife street of the French Quarter, best at dusk with neon lights.

text.description: Bourbon Street runs through the heart of the French Quarter, twelve blocks from Canal Street to Esplanade Avenue. It is best known for its bars, restaurants and music, but it also photographs well in daylight. Wrought-iron balconies, shuttered doorways and old brick and stucco fronts line both sides. Much of that look comes from the Spanish rebuilding after the Great New Orleans Fire of 1788, which is why the street feels more Spanish than French. The name itself dates from 1721 and honours the French royal House of Bourbon. Since the early 1970s the street has been a pedestrian mall, so you can stand and frame a shot without traffic, though the crowds can be thick later in the day. For a phone photo, the quietest option is early morning, when the street is nearly empty and the shutters are down. You get clean lines, the balconies and the full length of the street without people in the way. If you want the classic busy look, with neon, bars and balconies stretching into the distance, come back after dark and shoot down the strip. Another good frame is at Orleans Street and Bourbon Street, where the narrow street leads the eye to the back of St. Louis Cathedral. Keep your phone close and be aware of people around you in the evening.
text.geographic_location: Bourbon Street is in the French Quarter, the historic centre of New Orleans. It runs between Canal Street at one end and Esplanade Avenue at the other.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are listed for this spot. Walk along Bourbon Street, and check the day's barricade and closure status. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural street-level view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in the balconies and the full width of the street, and try telephoto (2x or more) to compress the street and pick out signs and ironwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Bourbon Street and Iberville Street. A quieter, emptier view of the street, useful when the crowds are gone. From here you get a quieter, emptier view of the street, which works best when the crowds are gone. Shoot along the street so the balconies and shutters line up on both sides, with the subject lying to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone level so the building edges stay straight. Use the balconies on each side as a frame leading down the street. If you want the classic neon-and-balconies view, take the long view down the strip from further along. A second option is Orleans Street and Bourbon Street, where the narrow street frames the back of St. Louis Cathedral.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the part of the street you want sharp, then slide the exposure down a little so bright signs and neon do not wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady. A Live Photo can catch movement in the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the street gets busy, when it is nearly empty and the shutters are down. For neon and atmosphere, go after dark, but expect crowds.

text.access_note: Bourbon Street is an open public street with a pedestrian mall, but access arrangements such as barriers or police presence have changed recently, so check the official city site and conditions on the day before you go.

name: The National WWII Museum
label: National WWII Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/12598945: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The National World War II Museum' (264 m across).
notes: Large museum campus in the Warehouse District.

text.description:
The National WWII Museum is a museum made up of several pavilions in the Central Business District, on Andrew Higgins Drive between Camp Street and Magazine Street. It began in 2000 as the National D-Day Museum and was named America's official National WWII Museum by Congress in 2003. The story starts with the Higgins boat, the landing craft designed and built in New Orleans, which is why the museum is here. Over the years new pavilions have been added, the latest being the Liberation Pavilion, which opened in 2023.

It photographs well because of the scale and the variety. The original Louisiana Memorial Pavilion has a tall atrium with a Supermarine Spitfire and a Douglas C-47 Skytrain suspended from the ceiling. A Higgins boat is usually on display below. The third floor has an observation deck for a closer look at the hanging aircraft. The US Freedom Pavilion: The Boeing Center is the largest building and holds bombers and fighters, including the B-17E My Gal Sal.

For phone photos, look up and look for layers: aircraft overhead, with visitors and exhibits below to give a sense of size. Outside, step back far enough to fit a whole facade in the frame. Ask a member of staff about photography rules inside, and check the official site for access details before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the Central Business District of New Orleans, on Andrew Higgins Drive between Camp Street and Magazine Street.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot, so head for the Central Business District and look for Andrew Higgins Drive, between Camp Street and Magazine Street. Once you arrive, the phone icon on the map is in the middle of the museum complex, so there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the atrium and the aircraft hanging overhead. Use the default lens (1x) for the building fronts and for people-sized details such as the Higgins boat. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single aircraft or marking without walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Photograph the buildings and open spaces nearby, and step back from any one building until its full height fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of walls and windows to keep them straight. Indoors, tilt the phone up slightly and shoot the hanging aircraft from the atrium floor, then try again from the third-floor observation deck for a closer, level view. Keep a person or an exhibit in the foreground for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the aircraft to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit areas don't wash out. In dim galleries, use night mode and hold the phone against your body or a rail to keep it steady. Use panorama only for the outdoor facades, as it distorts people and moving objects.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Inside, the light is much the same all day, so choose a quieter moment to get clear shots. For the outside of the buildings, morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for entry details and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The atrium and some galleries are likely to be dimly lit, so night mode may help.
Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light for outdoor photos.
The museum is likely to be quieter at certain times of day, and a quieter moment makes clearer photos.
Photography rules inside the museum may vary, so staff or the official site can confirm them.

name: Café du Monde
label: Café du Monde
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3362351943: the OpenStreetMap point 'Café du Monde'.
notes: Famous for beignets and café au lait since 1862.

text.description: Café du Monde is an open-air coffee shop on Decatur Street in the French Quarter, and it is one of the most recognisable stops in New Orleans. It is known for café au lait and beignets, which are square pieces of dough with no hole, served under a thick coat of powdered sugar. It started as a simple coffee stand in 1862 at the upriver end of the French Market, and the menu has changed very little since. It photographs well because the scene is lively and easy to read: the green and white colour scheme, the tables under cover, and the white sugar on dark plates and clothes. The coffee here is traditionally dark-roasted with chicory, and the café's orange-yellow coffee tins are a familiar sight too. Take a wide shot of the whole frontage first, so the café sits in its French Quarter setting. Then move in for close details such as a plate of beignets, a coffee cup or the sugar dusting. People will be moving about in front of you, so take a few frames and pick the one with the cleanest gaps. Wipe your lens before you start, because powdered sugar in the air tends to smudge it. Be polite about including other guests in your shots.
text.geographic_location: Café du Monde is on Decatur Street in the French Quarter of New Orleans, at the French Market site (800 Decatur Street). It sits at the upriver end of the market buildings.
text.directions_text: Head for the French Quarter and the French Market on Decatur Street. From there you look east towards the café. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the café frontage and its sign. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the street and the covered seating. Use 2x telephoto for beignets, cups and other close details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Decatur Street and St Ann Street (the café's front on the west side of Decatur, seen when walking north). The front of the original Café du Monde stand with its striped awning, framed by the Decatur Street sidewalk. From here the whole café is in front of you without you having to crowd the tables.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the café's roofline and sign along the top third. Keep the phone level so the building edges stay straight; with ultra-wide, avoid tilting it up. For a detail shot, move closer and use 2x rather than pushing the phone into someone's table.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the café to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the white sugar and signs do not blow out. Try portrait mode for a close-up of a plate or cup with a softened background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon are good for softer light and usually fewer people. Facing east, the morning sun will be roughly in front of you, so check the screen for glare.

text.access_note: Café du Monde is a working café open to the public, so check the official site before you go for current opening arrangements.
claims_not_in_sources: Standing west of the café and facing east, the morning sun will tend to be in front of you.
Early morning and late afternoon tend to be quieter and give softer light.
Powdered sugar in the air can smudge a phone lens, so it is worth wiping it.
Other guests will be moving around in front of the café while you photograph it.

name: Frenchmen Street
label: Frenchmen Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dat Dog' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Dat Dog' (way/1345337720): middle (24 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W12707084 (Frenchmen Street): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Live-music street in the Faubourg Marigny.

text.description: Frenchmen Street is a street in New Orleans that comes alive after dark, when live bands play in the clubs and sometimes out on the pavement. It photographs well because everything is close together: bright shopfronts, neon, strings of lights and people gathered around the musicians. The easiest picture is the colourful Dat Dog front at 601 Frenchmen St, with street life and a band outside. The Frenchmen Art Bazaar also has market stalls strung with lights, selling local artists' work. The crossing where bands often play makes a good view of the crowd around the musicians and the clubs lining the block. Photos from the street are generally fine. Inside clubs, follow each venue's own policy. Musicians often pass a hat, and a short clip is usually tolerated, but filming for a long time without tipping is frowned upon. Dusk and after dark are the best times, as the lights and neon come on. Keep your phone at chest height and watch for people walking through the frame. A tap on the brightest part of the scene stops the lights burning out.
text.geographic_location: Frenchmen Street is in New Orleans. It is known for its live-music clubs.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stop is listed nearby. Head to 601 Frenchmen St, where Dat Dog is. From there Frenchmen Street lies to the north, about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Dat Dog front and the crowd. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole shopfront and street in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a band across the street without walking into their space.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Dat Dog (exterior, facing the 601 Frenchmen St storefront). The brightly coloured Dat Dog front with street life and band activity on Frenchmen Street after dark. From here you get the bright front with street life and any band playing outside after dark. The street itself lies a short walk to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the Dat Dog front on one side, leaving the other side for people and the band. Keep the shopfront edges straight by holding the phone level. For a different shot, walk to the Frenchmen Art Bazaar for the lit stalls, or to the crossing where bands often play, for a view of the crowd around the musicians and the clubs along the block.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a lamp post or your elbows. Tap the brightest sign to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the neon keeps its colour. For a moving band, Live Photos or a short video clip works better than a long night exposure. Keep any clip short, and tip if you stay.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk and after dark, when the neon and string lights are on and the bands are playing.

text.access_note: Frenchmen Street is a public street, but club interiors follow each venue's own photo policy, so ask first or check the venue before you go.

name: Caesars Superdome
label: Superdome
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Poydras Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Poydras Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4598860: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Caesars Superdome' (367 m across).
notes: Huge domed stadium that dominates the skyline.

text.description: The Caesars Superdome, usually just called the Superdome, is the huge indoor stadium that dominates this side of New Orleans. It is home to the New Orleans Saints and opened in 1975. Its dome measures about 207 metres across and is the largest fixed domed structure in the world, so it is a very big subject for a phone. The best-known view is along Poydras Street, where the curved roofline and wall of the stadium rise up with the downtown office towers stacked behind. That mix of smooth curve and tall glass gives the picture scale and a clear sense of place. The building also has a story to tell. It sheltered thousands of people during Hurricane Katrina in 2005 and reopened in September 2006 after repairs, and it has hosted eight Super Bowls. Stand on Poydras Street and let the dome fill most of the frame, with the towers behind it. Late afternoon light suits it better than midday. If you want a second angle, Champions Square, the outdoor plaza next to the stadium, has the Rebirth statue and the Tom Benson statue as foreground subjects. The Poydras Street Bridge is said to give a raised view down over the I-10 towards the dome, but check the view on the spot. The stadium is not open for tours, so this is an exterior shoot. Allow extra time on event days, when crowds gather.
text.geographic_location: The Superdome stands in New Orleans, where Poydras Street runs towards it from the downtown office towers.
text.directions_text: Head for the Central Business District (CBD) and then walk west along Poydras Street towards the dome. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because the stadium is very large and the curved wall will not fit in the default lens (1x) from close by. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view with less stretching at the edges. Use telephoto (2x-5x) if you want to pull the office towers closer behind the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Poydras Street (approach heading west from the CBD toward the dome). The curved roofline and wall of the stadium framed against the downtown office towers behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Fill the frame with the dome and let the skyline stack up behind it. Switch on gridlines and keep the towers upright, so the curve is the only thing that bends. If you have time, Champions Square beside the stadium is a good alternative, with the Rebirth statue and the Tom Benson statue as foreground subjects.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the dome wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the curved wall keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light is softer than at midday.

text.access_note: The exterior Plaza Level is open to walk around, but the stadium is not open for tours and event days may bring crowds or restrictions, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the whole curve of the stadium in from close by.
Gridlines help keep the office towers upright in the frame.
Dragging the exposure slider down helps keep the sky from washing out.

name: Napoleon House
label: Napoleon House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chartres Street' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/331325950: the OpenStreetMap point 'Napoleon House'.
notes: Historic corner building and bar with a faded old-world look.

text.description: Napoleon House is a three-storey, stuccoed brick building on a corner of the French Quarter. It has a dormered hip roof, a small cupola on top and shallow ironwork balconies along the second floor. It photographs well because it looks like old New Orleans: plain, weathered walls, delicate ironwork and a rooftop lantern that rises above the neighbouring buildings. It was built in 1794 and enlarged in 1814. The name comes from a local legend that it was meant as a home for Napoleon Bonaparte after his exile, though the plan stopped when news of his death arrived in 1821. It was once the home of Nicholas Girod, a mayor of New Orleans, and has been a restaurant since 1914. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1970. The most flattering phone view is from Chartres Street, looking along the block, so the building sits in its street setting. A 1940 postcard framed it much the same way, showing parked cars in front and a church in the distance down the street. The postcard is historic, so check the current view on site. If you want the full corner façade and the cupola in one shot, step to the corner of Chartres Street and St. Louis Street instead. The courtyard and interior are popular with visitors, but they are inside a working restaurant, and the upper floors are apartments. So treat the street as your photo spot, and be considerate of diners and residents.
text.geographic_location: Napoleon House is at 500 Chartres Street, in the French Quarter of New Orleans, on the corner where Chartres Street meets St. Louis Street.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so head to 500 Chartres Street in the French Quarter. Once you are on Chartres Street, look for the three-storey corner building with the cupola and iron balconies. The phone icon on the map is right beside the building. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand on the corner and want the whole façade and cupola. Use the telephoto (2x or more) to pull the church at the end of the block closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Louis Cathedral. The 1940 postcard shows the building in its street setting, with parked cars and a church in the distance, so check the current view on site. For the full corner and cupola, move to the Chartres Street and St. Louis Street corner as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the building along one side of the frame, with the street leading the eye towards the church. Keep the phone level so the vertical walls do not lean. Wait for a gap between passers-by if you can. If you try the corner instead, include the cupola at the top of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building's wall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps some colour and the wall isn't too dark. Take a few frames, because passing people and cars change the scene quickly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter and gives softer light along the street, so check the view on site.

text.access_note: The street outside is public, but the courtyard and interior belong to an operating restaurant, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Preservation Hall
label: Preservation Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St. Peter Street' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Saint Peter Street and Royal Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/329365549: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Preservation Hall' (22 m across).
notes: Legendary traditional jazz venue on St. Peter Street.

text.description:
Preservation Hall is a jazz venue on St Peter Street in the French Quarter, and the street itself is a big part of the picture. The building began in the 1950s as an art gallery run by Larry Borenstein, who invited local jazz musicians to play for tips. The music soon drew more attention than the paintings. In 1961 it was renamed Preservation Hall, and it now welcomes roughly 180,000 visitors a year. That history helps explain why people often gather outside.

It sits on the St Peter Street corner at the hall's block and looks along the 700 block. You get the hall's building in the frame beside the French Quarter balconies and neighbouring buildings. It is also a quieter spot than standing in front of the door. If you want the close-up, walk a minute or so to the hall itself for the weathered street front and its hanging sign.

Keep your phone outside the door. Interior photography is not allowed during performances, and flash is prohibited, so plan on exterior shots only. Expect queues and a crowd on the pavement before showtimes. Be patient and wait for a gap, or shoot from the corner so the queue becomes part of the street scene. Check the official site before you go for current details.
text.geographic_location: Preservation Hall is on St Peter Street in the French Quarter, the old heart of New Orleans.
text.directions_text: The hall is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot. Street conditions can change, so check them before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street-corner view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the balconies are being cut off, and the telephoto (2x) for the hanging sign.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Saint Peter Street and Royal Street (corner at the Preservation Hall block, shooting along Saint Peter). A street-corner view of the 700 block of Saint Peter with the Preservation Hall building in the frame beside the French Quarter balconies and buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the verticals of the buildings straight. Let the balconies lead the eye toward the hall. Tilting the phone up too far makes the buildings lean, so hold it level and step back instead. For a different view, go to the hall's front and photograph the weathered facade and sign, with any crowd or musicians outside.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the front of the hall to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky or lit windows are washing out. Skip flash. It is prohibited inside, and it does little for a street scene anyway.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before or after shows is a sensible general suggestion, as the street may be calmer than during the pre-show queue. Dusk can give warm lights along the balconies; use night mode if it gets dark, and hold the phone steady against a wall or post.

text.access_note: The street corner is public, but the venue is a performance space where interior photography is not allowed during shows, so check the official site before you go.

name: St. Louis Cathedral
label: St. Louis Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jackson Square' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jackson Square' (way/27844554): middle (206 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/329364492: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathedral-Basilica of Saint Louis King of France' (85 m across).
notes: The three-spired cathedral that dominates Jackson Square.

text.description: St. Louis Cathedral is the white, three-spired church that closes off one side of Jackson Square in the French Quarter. It is also the part of New Orleans most people want in their photos. It is the oldest cathedral in continuous use in the United States, a title it shares with the Royal Presidio Chapel in Monterey, California, and it sits between the historic Cabildo and Presbytère. The first church here dates from 1718, the city's founding year. The second church burned in the great fire of 1788. The third church, built in 1789, was largely rebuilt in the 1850s, and the present structure dates mainly from 1850. The bell from 1819, named "Victoire", was reused and is still there. The best view is from the garden area of Jackson Square, facing the front on the Chartres Street side. From there the whole triple-spired facade fits in one frame, with the gardens around it and the Andrew Jackson statue as a foreground element. Guides often call this the most photographed spot in the French Quarter, so expect other people in your shot later in the day. The square is calmest at sunrise, and the floodlit cathedral looks good after dark. Walk a little to either side to change the angle, and watch the statue and lamp posts so they don't cut across the spires. The cathedral is an active parish. Photos are allowed outside Mass, but flash is not.
text.geographic_location: In the French Quarter of New Orleans, on the Chartres Street side of Jackson Square, facing the Mississippi River. It stands between the Cabildo and the Presbytère.
text.directions_text: Head for the French Quarter and Jackson Square. The spot data lists no station or tram stop nearby, so check local transport options yourself. The cathedral fronts the square on Chartres Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or want the statue and gardens in the foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spires and the clock.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jackson Square (garden area facing the cathedral's front (Chartres Street side)). The full triple-spired white facade framed by the square's gardens, with the Andrew Jackson statue as a foreground element. The cathedral lies to the north-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the spires up with the vertical lines. Put the statue low in the frame as a foreground element and let the facade rise above it. For an alternative, try Washington Artillery Park, across Decatur Street. It gives an elevated view over the square with the cathedral behind, and you can see the river and the Moonwalk from the same spot. The Moonwalk, the riverside walkway, shows the cathedral from the river side, framed by the square's gardens with the Mississippi in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the white stonework keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against something steady, or brace your elbows against your body, so the floodlit spires stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, when the square is empty and the facade has soft light. After dark is also good, for the floodlit cathedral.

text.access_note: The square and the exterior are open to view, but the cathedral is an active parish (photos are allowed outside Mass, with no flash), so check the official site before you go for services, events or closures.
claims_not_in_sources: Jackson Square is an open public square that can be walked into freely.
Holding the phone tilted upwards can make the spires look as if they lean inwards, so keeping the phone level helps.
Crowds are heavier later in the day than at sunrise.
Bracing your elbows or resting the phone on a solid surface helps keep night shots sharp.

name: Steamboat Natchez
label: Steamboat Natchez
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Woldenberg Riverfront Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Woldenberg Riverfront Park' (way/1548508457): edge nearest the subject (1638 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2486487251: the OpenStreetMap point 'Steamboat Natchez'.
notes: Paddlewheel steamboat docked on the Mississippi.

text.description:
The Steamboat Natchez is New Orleans' working paddlewheeler, and it is easy to recognise: a large sternwheel riverboat with a big wheel at the back, moored on the Mississippi at the edge of the French Quarter. She was built in 1975 and is about 265 feet (81 m) long. The wheel is made of white oak and steel and is 25 feet across. She also carries a steam calliope that can play 32 notes, so the boat can be heard as well as seen. She is sometimes called the Natchez IX, and she docks at the Toulouse Street Wharf. In 2022 a fire broke out on board, and she returned to service in 2023.

The boat photographs well because the river gives you a clear background. From the riverfront promenade you can include the water and the Crescent City Connection bridge behind the boat, which makes the picture look like New Orleans rather than just a boat at a quay. The long hull suits a wide frame. The calliope and pipes make a good close-up against the sky.

Start wide so the whole boat, the water and the bridge are in one picture, then step in for detail shots. Keep the horizon level using your gridlines. Cruise times change, so confirm the boat is in port before you go. The riverfront is also being rebuilt, so some stretches may be fenced off.
text.geographic_location: On the Mississippi riverfront at the edge of the French Quarter, in central New Orleans, at the Toulouse Street Wharf beside Woldenberg Riverfront Park.
text.directions_text: Head for the French Quarter riverfront and the foot of Toulouse Street (the boat's address is 400 Toulouse Street). Look for the large paddlewheel at the back of the boat. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole boat, the river and the bridge in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a tidier, more natural view. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the calliope, pipes and wheel.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Woldenberg Riverfront Park (riverfront promenade near where the steamboat docks). The paddlewheel steamboat moored at the riverfront, with the Mississippi and the Crescent City Connection bridge in the background. From there the paddlewheel steamboat is just to the south-east, with the Mississippi and the Crescent City Connection bridge behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the boat along the lower third, with the river and bridge filling the space behind. Keep the horizon level. For a different shot, move in close to the Steamboat Natchez itself and point the phone upwards to catch the steam calliope and pipes against the sky, with the paddlewheel side of the boat in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the boat to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white upper decks and the sky do not wash out. For the calliope, use telephoto (2x-5x) and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Whenever the boat is in port. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water, but cruise schedules change, so check the official site first.

text.access_note: The riverfront promenade is an outdoor public park, but it is being rebuilt, so check for closures; boarding the boat is a separate matter, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water.
Parts of the riverfront may be fenced off during the rebuild.

name: St. Louis Cemetery No. 1
label: St. Louis Cemetery 1
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Basin Street' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Basin Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: The oldest cemetery in the city, with above-ground tombs.

text.description:
St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 is the oldest of New Orleans' well-known cemeteries. It opened in 1789, after a fire in 1788 led to the city being redesigned, and it has been in use ever since. It covers only one square block, yet many thousands of people are buried here, mostly in above-ground tombs. The famous names include Marie Laveau, believed to lie in the Glapion family tomb, and Homer Plessy of the Plessy v. Ferguson case.

For most visitors the best free photo is from the street. The plastered brick wall along Basin Street was built with the same Spanish colonial methods as the tombs inside, and the tomb rows show just above it. The worn plaster of the brick wall, with the tomb rows just visible behind it, makes a good scene before you go in.

Getting inside normally means a guided tour, so check the official site before you go. Photography is generally welcomed on tours, but the tour guide's rules come first. If you only have time for the street, the corner of St. Louis Street and Basin Street frames the tomb walls against the Tremé streets. The Basin St. Station Visitor Information Center gives a wider view of the front wall and gate from across the road. Keep your phone close to your body while you wait for traffic to clear, and stay on the pavement.
text.geographic_location: The cemetery is on the north side of Basin Street, one block beyond the inland edge of the French Quarter, on the edge of Tremé. It is about eight blocks from the Mississippi River.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the French Quarter and head one block inland to Basin Street. Walk north-west along Basin Street to reach the cemetery wall. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long run of wall and the street. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the plaster and gate. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tomb rows above the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Basin Street (along the cemetery's exterior wall, before the entrance). The plastered brick outer wall of the cemetery with the tomb rows just visible behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Once you reach the wall, turn on the gridlines and line the top of the wall along a horizontal grid line, so the tombs sit neatly above it. For a different view, try the corner of St. Louis Street and Basin Street, or the Basin St. Station Visitor Information Center across the road for the wall and gate together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white plaster keeps its texture and the sky isn't washed out. Keep the phone level, as ultra-wide shots tilt walls easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the light is lower and softer, in the morning or late afternoon, to bring out the texture of the plaster. Quieter pavement times make it easier to stand back for a wide shot.

text.access_note: The street outside is open public pavement, but entry to the cemetery grounds is by guided tour only, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Softer morning or late-afternoon light tends to bring out the texture of old plaster.
The pavement along Basin Street can be busy with traffic and passers-by, so keep your phone secure.
Photography is generally welcomed on tours, but the guide's own rules apply.

name: Lafayette Cemetery No. 1
label: Lafayette Cemetery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Washington Avenue' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Washington Avenue and Prytania Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28328713: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lafayette Cemetery Number 1' (276 m across).
notes: Atmospheric 19th-century cemetery in the Garden District.

text.description:
Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 is a historic cemetery in the Garden District of New Orleans, founded in 1833 and the city's first planned cemetery. It sits inside a single city block and holds roughly 1,100 family tombs and about 7,000 people. The layout is a cross shape, designed to let funeral processions move through. It is known for its tombs and mausoleums, many built for several family members, and it has appeared in a long list of films and TV shows.

The most useful place for a phone photo is the corner of Washington Avenue and Prytania Street, outside the main gate. The white wall of sealed vaults, the iron gate and fence, and the tops of the tombs and oak trees behind them all fit into one frame. This corner is near Commander's Palace, and tour groups often gather at the gates. Because the tombs can be seen from the street, you can get a good picture without going in.

Access has changed over the years. The city closed the cemetery to visitors in September 2019, so check the official site before you go. If it is closed, the outside views still work well. Please stay on the public pavement, and leave drones at home, as flying them around cemeteries generally needs a permit.
text.geographic_location: Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 is in the Garden District of New Orleans, filling a city block at the corner of Washington Avenue and Prytania Street. Commander's Palace is close by.
text.directions_text: Start from the Garden District and head for the corner of Washington Avenue and Prytania Street. The St. Charles streetcar stops within a block of the cemetery. Street parking nearby is limited. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate and the wall of vaults. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole corner and the trees above it. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tomb tops and urns above the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Washington Avenue and Prytania Street (Outside the corner main gate, on the sidewalk across from the cemetery's white wall). The main gate and the wall-vault facade on Washington Avenue, with the tops of the tombs and oaks behind the iron fence.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the white wall up with a horizontal grid line so it doesn't slope. Put the gate on one third of the frame and let the oaks and tomb tops fill the rest. For a close, head-on picture of the sealed vaults, walk along Washington Avenue and zoom in on the vault roofs and urns above the wall. For a quieter angle away from the gate, try Prytania Street, where the tombs rise behind the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the wall doesn't turn pure white against the dark trees. Hold the phone steady with both hands, as you will not have a tripod.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late afternoon light usually suits the white wall best, and it tends to be calmer when tour groups are not at the gate.

text.access_note: The cemetery was closed to visitors in 2019, so check the official site before you go; the gate and wall can be photographed from the public pavement outside.

name: The Cabildo
label: The Cabildo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jackson Square' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jackson Square' (way/27844554): middle (206 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/329364483: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Cabildo' (62 m across).
notes: Former Spanish colonial government house next to the cathedral, now a museum.

text.description: The Cabildo was built as the seat of Spanish colonial city government and now forms part of the Louisiana State Museum. It stands on Jackson Square, right beside St. Louis Cathedral. The original building was destroyed in the Great New Orleans Fire of 1788, and it was rebuilt between 1795 and 1799. The Louisiana Purchase transfer ceremonies took place here in 1803. The mansard-roofed third floor was added in 1847, and the American eagle on the pediment replaced the Spanish coat of arms in 1821. A fire in 1988 destroyed the cupola and the whole third floor, and the building reopened in 1994. It photographs well because it sits in a row with the cathedral and the Presbytère, all facing the square, so one frame gives you history, symmetry and some greenery. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines so the tall facades stay straight. Then walk a minute or so towards the building for a closer shot of the eagle and the upper floors.
text.geographic_location: In New Orleans, on Jackson Square, directly next to St. Louis Cathedral.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so plan to walk to Jackson Square. The Cabildo lies to the west of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the Cabildo, cathedral and Presbytère together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or want more of the square's fence and trees in the frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the eagle on the pediment and the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jackson Square (from the square across Chartres Street, on the Chartres Street side). The Cabildo on the left of St. Louis Cathedral, with the Presbytère on the right, all facing the square. The Cabildo itself is just to the west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building edges up with the vertical lines. Let the square's fence and greenery fill the foreground, which makes a frame around the group of buildings. For a different view, Washington Artillery Park gives a higher overview of the square, the cathedral and the Cabildo.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building's facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright so the walls keep their colour. Check that the phone is level before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, when the square is empty and the light is soft on the cathedral facade.

text.access_note: You can photograph the building from the square, but museum entry and any access to the interior may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The square has a fence and greenery that frame the buildings when seen from the Chartres Street side.
Washington Artillery Park gives an elevated overview of the square.
Bright sky may make the facade look darker, so lowering the exposure helps (general phone photography advice).
The square is quietest at sunrise (one guide's tip).

name: Audubon Aquarium of the Americas
label: Audubon Aquarium
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/367725678: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Audubon Aquarium of the Americas' (194 m across).
notes: Large riverfront aquarium at the foot of Canal Street.

text.description:
Audubon Aquarium of the Americas sits on the Mississippi riverfront at the edge of the French Quarter, off Canal Street, at the upper end of Woldenberg Park. For a phone photographer it works in two ways. Outside, the Amazon exhibit is housed in a glass cylinder that stands out along the riverfront, so it gives you a simple, recognisable shape with water and sky behind it. Inside, the glowing blue tanks make colourful pictures.

The aquarium first opened on 1 September 1990 and focuses on aquatic life of the Americas. It reopened on 8 June 2023 after a $41 million renovation that brought the Audubon Insectarium into the same building. Among its roughly 10,000 animals are sharks, sea turtles and stingrays in the Gulf of Mexico tank. The Caribbean reef exhibit has a clear tunnel about 9 metres (30 feet) long, which is a good place for a picture with fish swimming overhead. The Mississippi River gallery includes a white alligator.

For the exterior, step back from the building in the park outside until the glass cylinder and the building fit together, with the river or sky in the frame. Indoors, light is low and glass reflects, so keep the phone close to the glass, shade the screen with your hand and avoid flash. Animals move constantly, so take a few shots, or use Live Photos, and pick the best one afterwards.
text.geographic_location: In New Orleans, at the edge of the French Quarter on the Mississippi riverbank off Canal Street. It stands at the upper end of Woldenberg Park.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Canal Street end of the French Quarter and head towards the river. From the park outside, the building and its glass cylinder are easy to spot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) from the park outside to fit the whole building and the glass cylinder in. Use 2x or more to pick out a single tank, a turtle or a ray from where you stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For an exterior shot, step back from the building in the park outside until the glass cylinder and the front fit in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the glass cylinder on one of the vertical lines, leaving the river or sky on the other side. Keep the phone level so the building does not lean. Inside, hold the lens almost touching the glass to cut reflections, and frame the Caribbean tunnel with the fish arching overhead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a fish or the animal you want to focus on, then slide the exposure slider down a little so the bright tank water does not wash out. Try night mode in dim galleries only if the animal is still, and avoid flash. Live Photos can help catch a moving shark or ray.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: For the outside, soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder than harsh midday sun. Inside, the tanks look the same at any hour, but a quieter time of day makes it easier to get clear shots.

text.access_note: The aquarium is run by the Audubon Nature Institute; check the official site before you go for entry details and any photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Entry details and photography rules inside the aquarium may vary, so the official site is worth checking.
Morning or late-afternoon light is usually softer for exterior photographs than midday sun.
The aquarium's galleries are dim and glass reflects, so flash is best avoided.
Stepping back from the building in the park outside lets you fit it in the frame.

name: Louis Armstrong Park
label: Louis Armstrong Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Congo Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Congo Square' (node/358384399): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28352381: large area 'Louis Armstrong Park' (739 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Park with the entrance arch and a statue of Louis Armstrong.

text.description:
Louis Armstrong Park is a 32-acre park in the Tremé neighbourhood, just across Rampart Street from the French Quarter. It was created after the 1960s urban renewal project cleared a large part of Tremé next to Congo Square, and it is named after New Orleans-born jazz legend Louis Armstrong. Inside you'll find the Municipal Auditorium, the Mahalia Jackson Theater for the Performing Arts and a 12-foot statue of Armstrong by Elizabeth Catlett. It also holds a bust of Sidney Bechet and a depiction of Buddy Bolden.

For photos, the best starting point is Congo Square, the part of the park in front of the Municipal Auditorium. It is known for its role in the history of African American music and spiritual practice. The ground is open, with a large oak tree and the auditorium behind, so it is easy to frame on a phone without fuss. The park also hosted the first New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival in 1970, and it has hosted events such as the free "Jazz in the Park" concert series. If you walk on, the park's lawns and water features and its entrance gateway make good alternative pictures. Congo Square can have weekend drumming and events, so expect people and performers in your shots. Take a few frames with and without them.
text.geographic_location: Louis Armstrong Park is in the Tremé neighbourhood of New Orleans, directly across Rampart Street from the French Quarter. Congo Square sits in front of the Municipal Auditorium inside the park.
text.directions_text: From the French Quarter, walk to Rampart Street and cross it to reach the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the square, the oak tree and the Municipal Auditorium together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the open ground and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the statues or a performer from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Congo Square (facing the Municipal Auditorium). The open Congo Square ground with a large oak tree, with the Municipal Auditorium in the background. The wider park lies to the north-east of this spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the oak tree on one third of the frame, with the auditorium behind it. Keep the horizon level and hold the phone at chest height for a natural view. For a different picture, try the park entrance from the street with its sculptured gateway and the greenery behind. Or look across the lawns and water features towards the downtown skyline from near the Mahalia Jackson Theater.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the oak tree or the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Live Photos can capture a little movement and atmosphere if there is music or drumming. If people are in the shot, take a few frames in a row.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the square is not too busy if you want clear shots of the ground and the tree. If you'd like the atmosphere of drumming and events, go at a weekend and expect people in your pictures.

text.access_note: This is a public park with a fence around it, so check the official site before you go for current access and any event restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: Congo Square may be quieter at times other than weekend events, which makes cleaner shots of the open ground more likely.
Dragging the exposure slider down can stop a bright sky looking washed out.
The park entrance gateway is best photographed from the street, as it is framed from there.

name: Royal Street
label: Royal Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Royal Street and Dumaine Street' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Royal Street and Dumaine Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Royal Street, New Orleans'.
notes: Elegant street of galleries and wrought-iron balconies.

text.description: Royal Street is one of the original streets of the French Quarter, dating from the early 18th century. It is known today for its antique shops, art galleries and hotels. It photographs well because the buildings are close together and lined with balconies, so a single frame can hold wrought-iron railings, shopfronts and painted facades all leading away from you. The corner of Royal and Dumaine is a good place to catch this. A balcony on the corner gives you a view north up the street, with the shops and colourful building fronts receding along the block. It is often a little quieter than the busier St. Peter Street corner, and the balcony is just as attractive. The street starts at Canal Street and runs on through the Quarter, and the upper part towards Canal Street is the one best known for its antiques. Because the street is busy through the day, it helps to be patient: wait for a gap in the people and then shoot. The balconies belong to private buildings, so take your photos from the public pavement and keep it clear for others. If you have time, the corners at St. Peter Street and St. Philip Street are also worth a look, with cast-iron balconies, hanging flower baskets and an angel detail on one of the galleried buildings.
text.geographic_location: Royal Street is in the French Quarter of New Orleans, starting at Canal Street. This spot is at the corner with Dumaine Street.
text.directions_text: There is no listed station or tram stop for this spot, so just head to the French Quarter and walk to the corner of Royal and Dumaine Streets. If you are already in the Quarter, follow Royal Street away from Canal Street until you reach Dumaine Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the balconies. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is too narrow to fit the whole facade. Try 2x if you want to pick out a single balcony or shopfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Royal Street and Dumaine Street (corner balcony, looking north up Royal Street). A balcony-lined stretch of Royal Street with its shops and colorful building fronts receding up the block.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the lines to keep the buildings upright. Put the balcony in the top corner of the frame and let the street lead the eye into the distance. If you also visit the St. Peter Street corner, you will find a similar view with flower baskets and cast-iron railings, and St. Philip Street has a sculpted angel detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a shaded building front to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the colours. Hold the phone still and shoot a few frames while people walk past, then pick the one with the clearest view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Royal Street is busy and crowded through the day, so check conditions before you go if you want a clear view.

text.access_note: This is an open public street, and the balconies are on private buildings, so shoot from the pavement and check local conditions before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Dumaine Street is a cross street of Royal Street in the French Quarter.
Shaded building fronts and a bright sky can make exposure tricky on a phone.

name: The Presbytere
label: The Presbytere
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jackson Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jackson Square' (way/27844554): middle (206 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4610716: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Presbytère' (69 m across).
notes: Colonial building on Jackson Square that houses a Mardi Gras museum.

text.description: The Presbytère is a two-storey brick building on Jackson Square in the French Quarter, standing right beside St. Louis Cathedral. It was designed in 1791 and finished in 1813 as a match for the Cabildo on the cathedral's other side. That pairing is what makes the square photograph so well: the three buildings form a balanced group, with the cathedral in the middle. The Presbytère has a nine-bay open arcade of elliptical arches on the ground floor, with matching arched openings above. The middle three bays are topped by a triangular pediment. The dormered mansard roof was added in 1847. The cupola on top was missing for many years and was put back in 2005, so the roofline you see today is complete. The building is a National Historic Landmark (designated 1970) and is now part of the Louisiana State Museum. For the classic photo, stand facing the cathedral, with the Presbytère on the right and the Cabildo on the left. Keep the cathedral spire in the middle of the frame and let the two side buildings balance it. If you want something closer, walk to the corner on Chartres Street. From there you can photograph the side wall and the arches, the pilasters and the window detail. Photos inside the museum are restricted, so plan on taking your pictures outdoors.
text.geographic_location: In the French Quarter of New Orleans, on Jackson Square, next to St. Louis Cathedral. It is the partner building to the Cabildo on the other side of the cathedral.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start in the French Quarter and head for the Jackson Square area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the cathedral, the Presbytère and the Cabildo into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view of the Presbytère beside the cathedral. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the cupola, the pediment and the arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jackson Square (from the square, facing the cathedral; the Presbytère is on the right). The Presbytère to the right of St. Louis Cathedral, framed across the square with the Cabildo on the left.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the cathedral's central spire on the middle line, so the two side buildings balance. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. For a different view, walk to the Chartres Street corner and photograph the side and corner façade with its arches and decorative details from close up.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the building does not look washed out. Take a few frames in case people walk through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is often calmer, so you may get fewer people in front of the building.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the public square; the Presbytère is a Louisiana State Museum, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside, where flash is prohibited and photography is restricted.

name: French Market
label: French Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jackson Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jackson Square' (way/27844554): middle (206 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4469406407: the OpenStreetMap point 'French Market'.
notes: One of the oldest public markets in the United States, along the river.

text.description:
The French Market is a long stretch of market buildings, shops and cafés running along six blocks of the French Quarter, just inland from the Mississippi. Part of the site has been used as a market since 1791, and the oldest surviving structures date to about 1813. It is described as the oldest market of its kind in the United States. The Works Progress Administration carried out major renovations in the 1930s, and work has carried on into this century. Many of the old open-sided stalls are now shops and restaurants.

It photographs well because of the long, low roofline, which draws the eye down the street. From the Decatur Street entrance of Jackson Square you get that view with a bit of space around you, away from the crush at the stalls. A short walk away you can also shoot the market's arch from the market side, or the river, docks and passing boats from the Moon Walk, with the back of the market behind.

The flea market is especially busy at weekends, and free music is often played here, so expect people in your frame. Keep your shots wide and let the crowd add life rather than trying to clear it. The roofline is a historical view, so check on your screen that the framing still works today. If you want close-ups of stalls, ask the vendor first, as not everyone is happy to be photographed.
text.geographic_location: The French Market is in the French Quarter of New Orleans, on the river side of the district, downriver from Jackson Square. It runs from the Café du Monde end towards the flea market stalls opposite the New Orleans Mint.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stops are listed nearby, so start from Jackson Square in the French Quarter and head north-east along Decatur Street with the market's roofline ahead of you. No public transport stops are listed nearby, so walk in from Jackson Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole roofline running down Decatur Street. Switch to 2x or the telephoto if your phone has one to bring the market closer and squeeze the buildings together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only when you are close to the arch or the arcade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jackson Square (the Decatur Street entrance, standing in front of the square). A view down Decatur Street toward the French Market, with the market's long roofline running along the street. From there you look down Decatur Street towards the market, which lies to the north-east, with its long roofline running along the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the edge of the roofline along a lower grid line so the street leads the eye into the picture. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. For a different view, the market's arch works from the market side, and the Moon Walk gives you the river and boats with the market behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the roofline to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the buildings keep their colour. Take a Live Photo if people are walking through, then choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light is recommended, but vendors may not be set up until around 10 am, so mid-morning may suit you better. Weekends are busier, especially with the flea market.

text.access_note: The street view from Jackson Square is in a public area, but individual shops, restaurants and stalls set their own rules, so check the official site before you go and ask before photographing vendors close up.

name: Pontalba Buildings
label: Pontalba Buildings
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St. Peter Street' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'St Peter Street' (way/12702800): point nearest the subject (1185 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/4610710: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lower Pontalba Building' (160 m across).
notes: Red-brick apartment buildings with cast-iron balconies flanking Jackson Square.

text.description: The Pontalba Buildings are two matching red-brick blocks that line the sides of Jackson Square in the French Quarter. Each is four storeys tall and a full block long. Baroness Micaela Almonester Pontalba had them built between 1849 and 1851, in the style of Parisian row houses. For photographers, the appeal is the repetition: a long brick front, rows of doorways and a lacy cast-iron gallery running along the upper floors. The galleries were the first recorded use of cast iron in this way in the city, and the balustrade panels carry the Baroness's initials, 'AP', woven into the pattern. The buildings were declared a National Historic Landmark in 1974. The ground floors hold shops and restaurants, and the upper floors are apartments. Peter Street. From there, facing Jackson Square on the upriver side, you look across the open lawn to the Lower Pontalba on the far side. The lawn gives you a clean foreground, and the long brick front sits behind it. Check the exact angle when you arrive. Shopfronts and signs at street level can creep into the picture, so keep the lens a little high and favour the galleries and brickwork. If you want a different view, walk into Jackson Square itself, where both buildings border the square, one on each side. Another option is the corner of Chartres Street and St. Ann Street, where you can photograph the Lower Pontalba's corner pillar from across the street.
text.geographic_location: The Pontalba Buildings stand in the French Quarter of New Orleans, on the two long sides of Jackson Square. The Upper Pontalba fronts St. Peter Street and the Lower Pontalba fronts St. Ann Street.
text.directions_text: Head for Jackson Square in the French Quarter. St. Peter Street runs along the upriver side of the square, and the Upper Pontalba stands on it. Stand on that street facing the square, and the Lower Pontalba is the long red-brick block across the lawn. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole brick front across the lawn. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include more of the square's plantings, and keep the buildings away from the edges of the frame, where lines can lean or stretch. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the cast-iron galleries and the 'AP' initials.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on St. Peter Street (facing Jackson Square, on the upriver side of the square). The Lower Pontalba building framing the far side of Jackson Square, with the square's open lawn in the foreground. Walk to St.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the long roofline with a horizontal grid line so the building doesn't tilt. Let the lawn fill the bottom third of the picture and the brick front the middle, and avoid the shop signs at ground level. For a second view, try Jackson Square itself, where both buildings border the square, or the corner of Chartres Street and St. Ann Street for the entrance pillar.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the red brick keeps its colour. Take a few shots with the telephoto of the ironwork and its pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the brick, and early in the day there are likely to be fewer people on the street.

text.access_note: The streets and Jackson Square are open public space, but the upper floors are apartments and the ground-floor shops and restaurants keep their own hours.
